meta.title: A whistle in cross-section
meta.summary: A moving pea helps give a whistle its trill. Ooh, come look at the tiny chamber behind that familiar sound.

sourceRefs.label: American Whistle Corporation: How Whistles Are Made
American Whistle Corporation: How Whistles Work

blocks.text: A pea whistle has a short route for air and a little room for movement. Air enters at the mouthpiece and passes through an opening into the chamber. A small sphere inside moves as the air passes, changing the sound into the familiar trill. American Whistle Corporation’s explanation of how whistles work describes the mechanism; its manufacturing account describes how the pea is placed inside before the mouthpiece is joined.

blocks.caption: A pea whistle in section. Air passes through the mouthpiece; the moving pea changes its sound into a trill. Simplified, not to scale.

blocks.text: If you have a metal whistle nearby, look for the mouthpiece, chamber, sound opening, seam, and ring. A diagram can help you follow the path, but the company’s account is still one maker’s description of its product. It says the finished whistle is hand-tested. No need to take one apart: follow the published cutaway, then listen to the next whistle you hear and picture the small sphere moving inside. I like that the space around the pea matters as much as the little sphere. Ooh, that familiar trill has become much more interesting.
